summary:
Massachusetts prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression in credit, public and private employment, union practices and housing under legislation enacted on 23 November 2011 and in force from 1 July 2012, following an executive order of 17 February 2011 that barred state government and its contractors from discriminating against transgender state employees. Public-accommodation coverage was added by a Senate vote of 33-4 on 12 May 2016 and a House vote of 117-36 on 7 July 2016, signed by Governor Charlie Baker and effective 1 October 2016, and was retained at the ballot on 6 November 2018 by 67.8 per cent to 32.2 per cent, the first statewide popular vote of its kind in the United States. For a visitor these are the operative rules in hotels, restaurants, shops, transport and other places open to the public.

Gender identity was written into the hate-crime statute with effect from 1 July 2012. The framework defines a hate crime as a criminal act accompanied by overt actions motivated at least in part by prejudice, including on grounds of gender and sexual orientation, and requires incidents to be collected, summarised and publicly reported through the Crime Reporting Unit created by the 1990 Hate Crimes Reporting Act, involving the State Police, the Attorney General and legislative committees, alongside a Governor's Task Force on Hate Crimes established in 1991.

The state issues its own identity documents on self-declared terms. Birth certificates may be amended to reflect gender identity without sex reassignment surgery. Non-binary X markers on driver's licences and state identification cards have been available since November 2019 under a Registry of Motor Vehicles regulation, and non-binary X birth certificates and amendment of gender on marriage certificates were authorised by law signed on 29 July 2024 in the FY25 budget. Marriage licence forms in Boston have carried no gender or sex field since August 2023. Name changes can be obtained confidentially without public notice under An Act Protecting Personal Security, signed on 25 November 2025.

Health care is protected in two directions. A shield law in place since 2022 protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where care lawful in Massachusetts was banned in the patient's home state; this is the provision most likely to matter to a visitor travelling from a state that has banned the care. In July 2022 both chambers passed and the Governor signed a bill codifying gender-affirming healthcare protections, which took effect immediately under an emergency clause rather than after the usual 90-day period. Conversion-therapy practices on minors were banned by legislation passed 147-8 in the House on 13 March 2019 and 34-0 in the Senate on 28 March 2019, enacted on 4 April 2019 and signed on 8 April 2019 with immediate effect, making Massachusetts the sixteenth state with such a ban.

Marriage is open to same-sex couples following the Supreme Judicial Court's ruling of 18 November 2003, with licences issued from 17 May 2004 after the 180-day legislative window; attempts at a constitutional amendment failed and ended in 2007. The 1913 bar on non-resident marriages was repealed on 31 July 2008, so a couple travelling to Massachusetts can marry there, and 2012 rulings treat out-of-jurisdiction civil unions and California registered domestic partnerships as equivalent to marriage.

Two provisions of the criminal code remain on the books unrepealed: section 34, criminalising the abominable and detestable crime against nature, and section 35, covering any unnatural and lascivious act. Private consensual adult conduct has been outside their reach since the Supreme Judicial Court's 1974 decision in Commonwealth v. Balthazar, and the provisions are unenforceable as applied to such conduct. Repeal attempts repeatedly stalled in committee, including through the 2018 session that removed the abortion, adultery and fornication laws but left the sodomy, anal-sex and oral-sex provisions; the Senate passed repeal unanimously in January 2024, the House advanced it in June 2025, and a Senate committee scheduled it for floor consideration on 24 July 2025. Massachusetts is the only New England state, and one of two northern states, that still carries legislative criminalisation of same-sex conduct. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls nominally within the statute's wording, though it is not enforced against private consensual conduct.

In a national legal-risk ranking published in July 2026, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and removal of legal recognition, Massachusetts sits in the fifteen-state Most Protective tier.
tangentialFactors:
The contrast within the July 2026 ranking falls on the laws of other states: repeat-offence bathroom provisions carrying up to five-year prison terms, as in Idaho, and an arrest policy for gender-identity bathroom use, as in Florida. Those measures belong to jurisdictions a visitor may be travelling from or through, not to the rules in force in Massachusetts.

The state's protection record and its criminal code point in different directions at once. Massachusetts was the second state to prohibit discrimination on sexual orientation, in 1989 after Wisconsin in 1982, and the first to authorise marriage for same-sex couples, in 2003, while leaving the offences its own 1974 ruling had made unenforceable on the books for more than fifty years.
localsOnly:
Parentage and adoption rules cover families formed without marriage. Second-parent adoption has been available since the 1993 ruling in In re Adoption of Tammy, visitation rights were recognised in July 1999, and exclusionary foster-parent regulations dating from 1985 were rescinded in April 1990 in settlement of a suit brought by Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders and the ACLU. Birth-certificate forms were changed from mother/father to mother/parent and father/parent in 2007 under Governor Deval Patrick, with standardised electronic hospital forms announced in February 2011. Legal parentage for children born through IVF and surrogacy, regardless of marital status, passed unanimously on 1 August 2024, was signed on 8 August 2024 and took effect on 1 January 2025.

Discrimination against LGBTI people in nursing homes was prohibited by a bill passed by the General Court in August 2024 and signed on 6 September 2024. Sexual orientation has been a protected ground in credit, employment, union practices, housing and public accommodation since 1989, was added to the 1983 hate-crime law in June 1996, and was recognised as a ground requiring scrutiny in jury selection by a Supreme Judicial Court ruling of August 2021. Anti-bullying legislation of May 2010 requires schools to adopt reporting, investigation and anti-retaliation procedures.
outOfScopeNotes:
The repeal of sections 34 and 35 was not completed in the sources reviewed. The Senate passed repeal unanimously in January 2024, the House advanced it in June 2025 and a Senate committee scheduled it for floor consideration on 24 July 2025; no enactment is recorded.

Several legislative dates and vote margins above rest on a general reference article rather than on enrolled texts, which have not been checked. The healthcare shield listing is current to 27 September 2026 and the legal-risk ranking to July 2026.

Massachusetts law binds state agencies, employers, landlords, service providers and public accommodations within the state. Entry screening, immigration custody and federal identity documents are not governed by state law and form no part of the findings above.
